findings.statement: The AI system is a high-risk AI system because it is intended to be used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life insurance, a use case listed in Annex III, and AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk.

The employee's ability to review the recommended premium does not remove the high-risk classification: even under the Article 6(3) derogation, an Annex III system that performs profiling of natural persons is always considered high-risk, and this system profiles applicants by analysing their medical and other personal data to assess risk.

As a deployer, the insurer must use the system in accordance with the instructions of use provided under Article 13 and must ensure human oversight of the system by natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority.

Before putting the system into service or using it at the workplace, the insurer must inform its workers' representatives and the affected workers, such as the employees reviewing premium recommendations, that they will be subject to its use.

Because it deploys an Annex III point 5(c) system that assists in making decisions related to the applicants, the insurer must inform applicants that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system.
The insurer must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment on the applicants before deploying the system, as a deployer of a system referred to in points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III.

The insurer must take measures to ensure, to its best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of its staff and other persons acting on its behalf, including the employees reviewing the system's outputs.

Applicants' medical information constitutes data concerning health, a special category of personal data, so the insurer's processing of it is prohibited under Article 9(1) unless an exception in Article 9(2) applies.

The applicants' right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal or similarly significant effects is engaged by the eligibility and premium determination; whether the employee's review takes the decision outside Article 22(1) depends on whether that review is a meaningful assessment rather than a formality, a matter the scenario does not settle.

Where the eligibility or premium decision is based on solely automated processing, it must not be based on health data unless the applicant's explicit consent under Article 9(2)(a) or an Article 9(2)(g) condition applies, together with suitable measures to safeguard the applicant's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests.

The insurer must carry out a data protection impact assessment prior to the processing because it involves a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, on which decisions affecting the applicants are based.

The insurer must inform applicants of the purposes and legal basis of the processing, including any Article 9(2) condition relied on for the health data, and of the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, referred to in Article 22(1) and (4), with meaningful information about the logic involved and the significance and envisaged consequences of the processing.
As an insurance undertaking, the insurer is a financial entity within the scope of DORA.

The insurer must govern the AI system within a sound, comprehensive and well-documented ICT risk management framework, for which its management body bears ultimate responsibility, since the system constitutes an ICT system composed of ICT software and services processing data.

summaries.relevance: Places the insurer's life-insurance risk assessment and pricing use case squarely within the high-risk list, anchoring the entire AI Act analysis.
Converts the Annex III listing into the operative high-risk classification from which the deployer obligations follow.
Precludes reading the employee-review step as removing high-risk status, since profiling keeps Annex III systems high-risk.
Fixes the insurer's core duty as deployer to operate the system within the provider's instructions of use.
Sets the standard of competence, training and authority that the insurer's human-review workflow must satisfy.
Adds a workplace-specific information duty towards the insurer's own employees before the system is put into service.
Creates the obligation to notify the applicants themselves that they are subject to this insurance AI system.
Imposes the pre-deployment fundamental rights impact assessment that applies to deployers of insurance risk-assessment and pricing systems.
Requires the insurer to build AI literacy among staff handling and reviewing the system's recommendations.
Supplies the definition by which the applicants' medical information is treated as health data for the Article 9 analysis.
Makes the insurer's processing of applicants' health data unlawful unless an exception applies, the central GDPR constraint on the underwriting process.
Frames the exception set from which the insurer must identify a valid condition for processing health data.
Governs whether applicants can resist the automated premium determination, with the employee review's meaningfulness as the decisive fact.
Restricts health-data-based automated decisions to explicit consent or a substantial-public-interest condition with suitable safeguards.
Requires the impact assessment to be carried out prior to the processing where risks to applicants are likely.
Names the profiling-based automated evaluation of personal aspects that this underwriting process performs as a DPIA trigger.
Requires disclosure of the legal basis, including any Article 9(2) condition, to the applicants.
Requires information about the automated decision-making and the logic behind the recommended premium.
Brings insurance undertakings within DORA, activating the ICT-resilience regime for the insurer's use of the AI system.
Supplies the definitions by which the AI system counts as an ICT system within DORA's material scope.
Assigns ultimate responsibility for ICT risk management, including the AI system, to the insurer's management body.
Requires the AI system's operational risks to be governed within a documented ICT risk management framework.

actions: Settle the insurer's role under the AI Act: whether it develops the system in-house, procures it, substantially modifies it or places its name or trademark on it, since Article 25 can convert a deployer into a provider with the corresponding Chapter III obligations.
Determine the GDPR lawful basis under Article 6(1), the Article 9(2) condition relied on for the health data, and whether further national conditions under Article 9(4) affect that processing.

Establish whether the employee's review of the recommended premium is a genuine, weighted assessment, which decides whether the premium decision is based solely on automated processing under Article 22(1).
Verify the sources of the medical information analysed, since data obtained from third parties rather than from the applicants triggers the Article 14 information duties in addition to Article 13.

Confirm whether the insurer qualifies for a DORA Article 2(3) exclusion as a small, non-interconnected insurance undertaking, and whether the AI system is supplied by an ICT third-party service provider, which would engage DORA Articles 23, 28 and 30.
